questions.prompt: A plate defines `spacing = (width - 2 x margin) / (holes - 1)`. With width = 140 mm, margin = 12 mm, and holes = 5, what is the spacing between adjacent holes in millimeters?
questions.explanation: (140 - 24) / 4 = 116 / 4 = 29 mm; changing a parameter recomputes the spacing automatically.

questions.prompt: A sketch line starts with 4 degrees of freedom. You pin one endpoint to the origin with a coincident constraint and add a length dimension. How many degrees of freedom remain?
questions.explanation: The coincident constraint removes 2 DOF and the length removes 1, leaving 1: the free endpoint can still swing around a fixed-radius arc.

questions.prompt: Editing an early feature in the feature tree forces every feature listed after it to recompute.
questions.explanation: Each later feature is built on the geometry left by earlier ones, so a change propagates down the tree.

questions.prompt: A free part has 6 degrees of freedom. A pin gets a concentric mate to a hole (removing 4 DOF), then a coincident mate between its shoulder face and the bracket face. Since the tilts are already removed, that second mate only removes the remaining axial translation. How many DOF remain?
questions.explanation: 6 - 4 = 2 remain (slide along the axis, spin about it). The coincident mate removes only the slide, leaving 1 DOF: the pin can still spin.

questions.prompt: Match each assembly mate to what it does.
pairs: Forces two faces to touch flush
Makes two cylindrical features share one axis
Fixes a specific offset between two faces
Fixes a specific angle between two faces or axes
questions.explanation: Each mate removes a different set of freedoms, encoding what should stay true about the design.

questions.prompt: Which practice best preserves design intent when building a feature tree?
choices: Add refinement features such as fillets and chamfers toward the end of the tree
Reference the edges created by fillets for later sketches
Put fillets first so later features snap to them
Avoid naming or ordering features deliberately
questions.answer: Add refinement features such as fillets and chamfers toward the end of the tree
questions.explanation: Refinement features get tweaked most, so putting them last means nothing is built on them to break.

questions.prompt: Three parts are stacked end to end with tolerances of ±0.04 mm, ±0.06 mm, and ±0.01 mm. What is the worst-case total tolerance of the stack, in mm (±)? Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Worst-case stack-up is the sum of the tolerances: 0.04 + 0.06 + 0.01 = 0.11 mm.

questions.prompt: A hole ranges from 20.00 mm to 20.03 mm. A shaft ranges from 20.04 mm to 20.06 mm. What type of fit is this (clearance, transition, or interference)?
questions.explanation: The hole's largest size (20.03) is still smaller than the shaft's smallest size (20.04), so the shaft is always larger and must be pressed in.

questions.prompt: Locating a hole with separate ±0.10 mm x and y dimensions creates a square tolerance zone that allows more deviation along the diagonal than along either axis.
questions.explanation: A square zone reaches farther toward its corners, which is why a round position tolerance zone is more consistent in every direction.

questions.prompt: A PLA tab carries 120 N through a 4 mm x 5 mm cross-section. PLA's yield strength is 60 MPa. What is the factor of safety? (Use σ = F/A and FS = yield strength / σ.)
Which statements about design for manufacturability are true?
choices: Draft angles help a part release from a mold
Minimum wall thickness depends on the manufacturing process
An undercut can block a part from being made cleanly by a given process
Draft angle is required for FDM 3D printing
A CAD file that renders correctly is guaranteed to be manufacturable
answers: Draft angles help a part release from a mold
Minimum wall thickness depends on the manufacturing process
An undercut can block a part from being made cleanly by a given process
questions.explanation: DFM rules come from the physical process; draft matters for molding, not FDM, and CAD software does not check them.

questions.prompt: Explain why a 3D-printed part's real strength is usually lower than its material's published strength, and what a designer should do about it.
rubric: Says published values describe fully solid bulk material
Says printed parts are fused layers and often partial infill
Gives the typical reduction (roughly 60 to 80% of bulk strength) or says it depends on orientation and settings
Says to derate the strength before computing the factor of safety, and test safety-critical parts
questions.model: Published strengths describe solid bulk material, but a printed part is built from fused layers and often less than 100% infill, so it typically reaches only about 60 to 80% of that value depending on orientation and settings. A designer should derate the strength before computing the factor of safety, and physically test anything safety-critical.
questions.explanation: Layer bonding and infill reduce real strength, so derating gives a more honest factor of safety.

questions.prompt: A part is 30 mm tall and is printed at a layer height of 0.15 mm. How many layers does the print have?
questions.explanation: Number of layers = part height / layer height = 30 / 0.15 = 200.

questions.prompt: As a rule of thumb, FDM surfaces within about 45° of vertical usually print cleanly without support material.
questions.explanation: Steeper surfaces self-support; shallower, more overhanging ones generally need supports.

questions.prompt: Match each FDM print problem to its description.
pairs: Corners lift off the bed from uneven cooling and shrinkage
Thin wisps of plastic between separate features
Layers suddenly offset partway through, usually a mechanical issue
The first layer fails to stick reliably
questions.explanation: Most of these trace to design or setup choices that can be fixed before printing.

questions.prompt: A laser cutter has a kerf of 0.2 mm. A slot should end up exactly 8.0 mm wide after cutting. What width, in millimeters, should the slot be drawn in the file?
questions.explanation: A slot opens up by one kerf when cut, so draw it kerf narrower: 8.0 - 0.2 = 7.8 mm.

questions.prompt: Tabs and slots are drawn at the same nominal width and cut with a kerf of 0.1 mm. What is the total slop in the joint?
questions.explanation: The tab comes out one kerf too small and the slot one kerf too large, so the mismatch is 2 x kerf = 0.2 mm.

questions.prompt: A small phone-stand bracket is flat (no compound curves) and you need 5 copies. Explain why laser cutting is a better choice than FDM printing here.
rubric: Says the design is flat so laser cutting can produce it
Says all 5 parts nest on one sheet and cut in one short job, versus sequential multi-hour prints
Says kerf-compensated laser cutting gives tighter, more repeatable tolerances for the slot
Mentions raster engraving can add a label or logo in the same job
questions.model: The bracket is flat, so laser cutting can make it. All five parts nest on one sheet and cut in minutes, while FDM prints them one at a time over hours. Once kerf-compensated, laser cutting also holds the slot tolerance more tightly and repeatably, and raster engraving can add a label in the same job.
questions.explanation: Laser cutting wins when the geometry is flat because of batch speed and tolerance, and FDM's compound-curve advantage is not needed.
